body:
You are drafting spoken lines for a video game. Reply with plain text only, in the exact row format given at the end of this message. Do not send messages to anyone else and do not ask questions: decide. Write nothing but the rows (no title, no notes, no Markdown).

THE GAME. "The Crooked Moon" is a single-player, turn-based tactical party RPG built from a folk-horror Dungeons and Dragons campaign. It is set in Wickermoor Hollow, a haunted valley in Druskenvald, a land of endless night under a giant Crooked Moon with a crone's face. The look is a Halloween that never ends, drawn like an 1980s cartoon. A ghost train, the Ghostlight Express, has crashed in the valley; the party is stranded in the Hollow and its village, Wickermoor. The tone is warm, wry and funny on the surface, with real dread and real grief underneath. The player controls a party of four chosen from six companions: Rook Coldwake, Tobin Hayward, Silas Vane, Delphine Ravelle, Lucan Houndstooth and Cordelia Skein. They are quirky, capable adults.

THE NARRATOR. A NARRATOR row is spoken by the Vagrant, the green-skinned ferryman of the ghost train, who tells the tale in a folksy Southern drawl. At the camp fire he is warm and wry, and when a talk turns sad his humour leaves and he goes plain and level. He speaks to the party as "you" and about the companion in the third person, by first name. Present tense, one or two sentences, under about 32 words. Concrete senses (a smell, a sound, a touch, what the hands are doing) over adjectives. Never tell the player what to feel. Never "suddenly". No facts the party could not see. Drop the final g ("hangin'") in about one Narrator row in four, and use no other dialect spelling. He is kind, never mocks a stumble and never makes light of the dead.

RULES FOR EVERY LINE.
1. The companion's voice sheet below comes first. Match its accent, pace, vocabulary and contractions, and the existing lines. Use a pet phrase at most twice in the whole reply and never twice in one talk. Never repeat or closely paraphrase a line already in the voice sheet or the note.
2. A SAY row is the companion speaking: one or two short sentences, under about 28 words. Never put three sentences in one row; start another row instead.
3. The party's options (OPTION rows) are under 12 words, in the plain voice of the party, work at any hour and in any weather, never name a hero, and are never rolls or checks. A reply must always answer the option it follows.
4. Canon limits. Use only the facts in the voice sheet and the note below. Do not invent a new named person, place, monster, event, object the companion carries, or piece of the companion's history. You may invent small, harmless habits, fondnesses, superstitions and turns of phrase, and the look of the fire and the night. Name no place that the note does not name. Never state a dark secret. You may come close to one and step back.
5. Nothing here is a game system: no dice, no checks, no points, no levels, no HP, no "approval", no menus talked about aloud. Plain punctuation only (commas, full stops, hyphens, apostrophes, question marks, quotation marks inside a line when someone is quoted). No em dashes, no semicolons, no brackets, no asterisks, no stage directions, no placeholders.
6. Humour comes from the character, never explained. The sad turn is plain and short.
7. Our own words. Nothing quoted from any book.

THIS REQUEST. Three camp talks for Cordelia, as the party earns Cordelia's trust: a small secret, what Cordelia wants, and what Cordelia would give up for the party. The companion is CORDELIA SKEIN (call them Cordelia in NARRATOR rows). The attached note is the voice sheet and the fact sheet; it describes an older plan for the Thread's beats in places, so take people, objects, manner and background from it, but where it disagrees with THE FIXED FACTS in this brief, the fixed facts win.

HOW A CAMP TALK WORKS. After a rest the player can walk up to a companion who has asked for a word at the fire. It is private, short and warm. The companion speaks first (NARRATOR and SAY rows), the player chooses what the party says from three short options (or two where the talk says so), and the companion answers in their own voice (a REPLY). Then the talk ends. Nothing in it is a roll or a failure, and every reply must leave the talk finished and the fire going: a cool reply is still an ending, never a slammed door. Each reply also carries a REASON row: one sentence beginning "You", past tense, under 14 words, saying what the party did or said as the companion would remember it (for example "You heard me out at the fire" or "You waved it off and went to bed"). A REASON is plain notice text and is not spoken.

THE TALKS. Write these three talks, in this order, with these keys. Each is a private word at the fire.

TALK warm. Cordelia is glad to be travelling with the party and tells them a small secret: a habit, a fondness, a silly superstition or a soft spot they keep from others, NOT the dark secret and nothing from the note's dark-secret section, and not a topic the note's existing camp talks already cover. It must be a thing the party could laugh with them about, and it still says something true about them. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 6 to 8 SAY rows. Three options: OPTION 1 asks them to say more; OPTION 2 keeps the confidence kindly; OPTION 3 teases them about it (cheerfully, never cruel). Replies of 1 to 3 rows, each with a REASON row.

TALK close. Cordelia trusts the party with what matters most: what they want. Their wish, from the note and the game's journal: Finish the change someone else began in her, on her own terms. Say it in their own words, as a hope rather than a plan, and say what the road has done to that wish. No new facts about their past. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 6 to 8 SAY rows. Three options: OPTION 1 promises to help; OPTION 2 asks what it would take; OPTION 3 doubts it kindly, wondering if it is enough. Replies of 1 to 3 rows, each with a REASON row; the doubting reply still ends warmly.

TALK devoted. Cordelia would follow the party up the Crooked Tree and back down again, and says what they would give up for it: something dear to them, from the note, named plainly and without grand speeches. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 6 to 8 SAY rows. Three options, all kind: OPTION 1 says the party would do the same; OPTION 2 tells them not to give that up; OPTION 3 simply thanks them. Replies of 1 to 3 rows, each with a REASON row AND an INSPIRE row: INSPIRE is four to seven words, past tense, no name, saying what Cordelia did in this talk (for example: gave the party their word).

THE ROW FORMAT (exact). One row per line, rows in this order, nothing else:

TALK <key>
NARRATOR: <line>
SAY: <line>
SAY: <line>
OPTION 1: <what the party says>
OPTION 2: <what the party says>
OPTION 3: <what the party says>
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: <optional line>
SAY: <line>
REASON: You <what the party did>
REPLY 2
...
REPLY 3
...

TALK <key> starts a talk (the keys are given below, exactly). The rows before the first OPTION are the talk's opening. Each REPLY block holds one optional NARRATOR row first, then one or two SAY rows, then a REASON row (and an INSPIRE row where the talk asks for one). Write exactly the talks listed, in the order listed, with the row counts given.

The TALK keys, exactly: warm, close, devoted.

ATTACHED DOCUMENTS. Two documents come attached to this message; read both before you write. `tasks/crooked-moon-companions/cordelia_skein-voice-and-beats.md` holds the voice sheet for CORDELIA SKEIN (age, accent, pace, pet phrases, existing lines) and the character file (what Cordelia likes and dislikes, the Thread, the dark secret you must never state). `tasks/crooked-moon-companions/cordelia_skein-camp-talks.md` holds the camp talks already written for Cordelia, as voice examples: do not repeat their topics or lines.
result:
TALK warm
NARRATOR: Cordelia sits near the embers with four lower hands tucked into her waistcoat, rollin' a tiny bead of cooled candle tallow between two fingertips.
SAY: I must confess a minor methodological failing, darling, as your company has made me alarmingly lax with my evening protocols.
SAY: Look at these lower four hands, idling in my lap like four bored students at the back of a lecture hall.
SAY: Whenever my primary pair is occupied with a pestle or a teacup, the others grow terribly restless without a task.
SAY: Left to themselves, they begin braiding whatever falls within reach, from bootlaces and blanket fringes to loose strands of moss.
SAY: Back in Nerukhet, an unscheduled movement on the bench was treated as a regression of the nervous system.
SAY: Out here by the fire, I have caught my lowest left fingers secretly plaiting little decorative knots into the edge of my cloak.
SAY: It serves zero anatomical purpose, yet I find I lack the academic rigour to untie them before bed.
OPTION 1: Tell us what else those spare hands get up to.
OPTION 2: Your secret is safe by this fire.
OPTION 3: Keep them away from our bootlaces while we sleep.
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: Two of her lower fingers flick out and tie a neat double bow in a dry blade of grass before she stills them.
SAY: Yesterday they sorted a pouch of salt by crystal geometry while I was trying to read Doctor Hespa Marlowe's margins.
SAY: It is a soothing little pathology, truth be told, when nobody is grading the specimen.
REASON: You asked to hear more about my restless extra hands.
REPLY 2
SAY: How remarkably discreet of you, darling, to overlook such frivolous needlework in a serious researcher.
SAY: It is rather pleasant to travel with colleagues who do not audit every twitch of my thorax.
REASON: You promised to keep my small habit to yourself.
REPLY 3
NARRATOR: All six of Cordelia's eyes narrow in bright amusement as she taps her ruby-glass vials.
SAY: Do hold still, this will only tingle if I decide to braid your cuffs together before dawn.
SAY: Though I promise to restrict my illicit macrame to my own hems until breakfast.
REASON: You teased me about braiding the camp's bootlaces.
TALK close
NARRATOR: Cordelia holds a page of water-stained notes toward the firelight, watching a diagram of crimson silk-thread shimmer in the heat.
SAY: When Provost Alaric Glass first altered my humours in the caverns, he designed a specimen that required constant calibration just to stay awake.
SAY: Every vial plugged into my thorax is a borrowed measure, an unfinished equation written by someone else's knife.
SAY: I came into this valley chasing Doctor Hespa Marlowe's final treatise because I refused to remain another scholar's rough draft.
SAY: My hope has always been to finish the change they began in me, cleanly and entirely on my own terms.
SAY: Before this road, I imagined that perfection meant sealing myself behind cold glass where nothing could ever shift my ratios again.
SAY: Travelling beside you has altered the hypothesis, darling, in a way my margins never accounted for.
SAY: I no longer wish to be a sterile monument to transmutation, only a whole creature who owns her own waking mind.
OPTION 1: We will help you finish the work on your terms.
OPTION 2: What will it take to stabilise the change for good?
OPTION 3: Will perfecting the formula truly let you rest?
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: She folds the monograph carefully and slips it back inside her charcoal silk waistcoat.
SAY: Having peer reviewers who care whether the researcher survives the experiment is a novel luxury.
SAY: With your steadiness at my elbow, I believe my final calibration will hold.
REASON: You promised to help me complete my change on my own terms.
REPLY 2
SAY: A reagent that does not decay like common blood, and the nerve to rewrite the Provost's baseline from the marrow up.
SAY: The assay will be delicate, darling, yet my hands have never been steadier than they are in this camp.
REASON: You asked what it would take to finish my work.
REPLY 3
NARRATOR: The crimson thread between her fingers dissolves into faint red mist as she looks into the coals.
SAY: Perhaps no formula cures a restless intellect, darling, and I shall always find another ratio to test.
SAY: Still, it will be a profound relief to know the breath in my lungs belongs solely to me.
REASON: You wondered kindly whether finishing the formula would bring me peace.
TALK devoted
NARRATOR: Cordelia sets her lead-lined jar on a flat stone by the fire, her six eyes clear and unblinking in the amber light.
SAY: We are marching toward the roots of the Crooked Tree, and I have been calculating the odds of our little expedition.
SAY: You have never once looked at my six eyes or my thorax vials as a curiosity to be catalogued or pitied.
SAY: For all my talk of clinical detachment, I find my priorities have undergone a rather drastic recalibration.
SAY: I have carried Doctor Hespa Marlowe's monograph and this calibration jar as if they were the only bridge out of the dark.
SAY: If the work ahead demands a price, I would smash every vial of my research and empty the Provost's jar into the ash to keep you standing.
SAY: Let the Apex Humour go unwritten if it must, darling.
SAY: I would rather walk into the fog with an unfinished thesis than lose a single pulse around this fire.
OPTION 1: We would give up just as much for you.
OPTION 2: Keep your notes safe, we will survive together.
OPTION 3: Thank you for standing with us to the end.
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: She rests two lower hands lightly over the brass latch of the jar, her mouth curving in a quiet smile.
SAY: Fascinating pathology, that a handful of travellers can outweigh a lifetime of laboratory ambition.
SAY: Let us make sure neither side of the ledger has to pay that tuition tomorrow.
REASON: You said the party would sacrifice just as much for me.
INSPIRE: Put the party above her lifework.
REPLY 2
SAY: A sound hypothesis, darling, and one I intend to test with every alchemical trick in my coat.
SAY: Still, the ratio is fixed in my mind if the equation ever turns against us.
REASON: You told me not to give up my research for the party.
INSPIRE: Swore to put the party first.
REPLY 3
NARRATOR: Cordelia inclines her head, the ruby-glass vials at her chest catchin' the steady glow of the coals.
SAY: Gratitude is unnecessary among colleagues, darling, though it warms the humours all the same.
SAY: Do get some rest before we test the tree's anatomy in the morning.
REASON: You thanked me for standing with the party.
INSPIRE: Pledged her loyalty at the fire.
